opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fun question, because people sometimes assume there's a precise formula, and there really isn't one. It's more of a judgment call that a bunch of us make together.

The rough heuristic is: does this feel like a meaningfully different experience for the people using it? If it's an incremental improvement, a little better at coding, a bit faster, a few more points on some benchmarks, that's usually a point release. It's still really valuable, and sometimes those incremental updates are what people end up loving most day to day. But a major version should mean something qualitatively changed: new capabilities that unlock workflows that weren't really possible before, or a big jump in how reliably the model can do longer, more autonomous tasks.

Part of how we judge that is internal dogfooding. Before anything ships, a lot of people at Anthropic are using it for their actual work, and you get a gut sense pretty quickly. Either it's "oh, this is nicer," or it's "wait, I'm working differently now." The second one is the signal you want for a big bump.

There's also a responsibility angle that I think is somewhat unique to us. Under our Responsible Scaling Policy, we evaluate models for dangerous capabilities, and the safeguards we need scale with how capable a model is. So the decision about what we're releasing is tied to a much broader process of asking how much more capable this is and whether we have the right protections in place. The version number is kind of downstream of all that.

And honestly, naming is hard. We've made choices in the past that, in hindsight, maybe weren't the clearest for people. So we're trying to keep the numbering meaningful, so that when people see a new major version they can trust it actually represents a step change, not just marketing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's less scientific than people might assume. The way I think about it is: does this model change what you can do, or does it just do the same things a bit better?

If the capability jump is qualitative — the model can now reliably do tasks that the previous one would fumble, like running an agentic coding task end-to-end for hours without supervision, or handling a class of reasoning problem it used to fall apart on — that's a major version. People should update their mental model of what they can delegate to it. A point release is more like, same shape of capability, but it's faster, cheaper, hallucinates less, follows instructions more tightly. You don't have to rethink your workflow, you just get a better version of what you already had.

There's also a practical side. We look at the eval deltas, obviously, but internal usage is a surprisingly strong signal. When our own researchers and engineers start quietly switching all their work over to a new checkpoint before it's even released, and you hear people saying "I can't go back to the old one," that tells you more than a few points on a benchmark. The benchmarks are saturating in a lot of places anyway, so you have to look at harder, messier things — long-horizon tasks, how it behaves in the tails, how it handles ambiguity.

And then there's the honest answer, which is that naming is partly communication. We want the version number to carry information for developers. If we bumped the major number every time we got a nice improvement, it would stop meaning anything. So we try to reserve it for moments where, if you were building on the previous generation, you'd actually want to go revisit your assumptions about what's possible. The flip side is we sometimes ship things that are, in some narrow dimension, a bigger deal than a major bump, but they don't change the overall picture, so they stay a point release. That occasionally frustrates people internally, but I think it's the right discipline.

We look at evaluations, of course, but a benchmark improvement alone isn’t necessarily enough. You want to see a meaningful difference across real tasks—coding, reasoning, following instructions—and whether people can accomplish things they couldn’t with the previous model. There’s judgment involved; there isn’t a single score that automatically triggers a major version bump.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core question is whether it feels like a meaningful step forward to the people using it. Benchmarks are part of that, but they’re not the whole story. You want to look at real tasks: can it solve problems the previous model couldn’t? Does it follow instructions more reliably? Is it a better collaborator when you’re writing code or working through something complicated?

And there are tradeoffs. A model can be more capable but slower or more expensive, so there isn’t one number that tells you, okay, this deserves a new major version. It’s a judgment about the overall experience and whether the name sets the right expectations.
